title: Go Daemon Hardening: Process Isolation, Capability Dropping, and the Privilege Escalation Surface Inside Your Service
description: How Go daemons accumulate privilege surface, and the Linux primitives—capabilities, namespaces, seccomp—that close it before an attacker does.
linkedin_post:
Most Go services are over-privileged by default—not because of bad intentions, but because the path of least resistance is to hand the process whatever the container runtime provides and move on.

The attack surface that creates is real: a deserialization bug, a confused-deputy in an internal RPC, or a path traversal can turn into full host compromise when the process still holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE and an unrestricted syscall vocabulary at runtime.

In my latest article, I work through the concrete Linux privilege primitives a Go engineer can engage at startup to close that surface before an attacker does:

→ Why the privilege lifecycle has three distinct phases (startup, transition, runtime) and why the ordering of syscall.Setgroups / Setgid / Setuid matters at the kernel level
→ How LockOSThread interacts with per-thread credential changes in Go's M:N threading model—and the footgun that leaves other goroutines unaffected
→ Seccomp allowlist construction for Go daemons, including why a filter derived from pure-Go profiling will kill a cgo-linked binary under load
→ The PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS bit, ambient capability inheritance, and why neither a uid drop nor a Kubernetes securityContext alone is sufficient
→ A practical decision framework: audit → bind early → zero capabilities → set no-new-privs → install seccomp → validate in the readiness probe

This is not a platform concern you can delegate to your cluster's admission controllers. The privilege contract lives in the binary, and it needs to be enforced there.
